chapters.n: Deuteronomy is Moses’ farewell — a series of sermons to the new generation on the east side of the Jordan. The place names locate the camp, though several are now uncertain.

f.g: East of the Jordan River, in Moab, from the writer’s viewpoint across from Canaan.
Hebrew Suph; here probably a place name rather than the sea itself.

chapters.n: A sad aside: the trip from Mount Sinai (Horeb) to Kadesh-barnea, the doorway to Canaan, takes only eleven days. Unbelief turned it into forty years.

f.g: Deuteronomy’s usual name for Mount Sinai.

chapters.n: Moses speaks on the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year — about two months before Israel crosses the Jordan. He teaches all the Lord commanded.
This comes after the victories over Sihon and Og, proof that God can conquer powerful kings.

f.g: Ashtaroth, a city in Bashan named after a Canaanite goddess.

chapters.n: In Moab, Moses begins to “declare” — to explain and make plain — the law. Deuteronomy means “second law” in Greek: not a new law, but the old one retold.
Moses begins his review: at Horeb the Lord said they had stayed long enough at the mountain. It was time to move forward.

f.w: Ye have dwelt long enough in this mount

chapters.n: God told them to head for the hill country of the Amorites and all of Canaan — even as far as Lebanon and the Euphrates. The promise was vast.

f.w: the great river, the river Euphrates

chapters.n: The land had already been placed before them; they only needed to go in and take it. God had sworn it to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Moses recalls telling them he could not carry the load of leading them alone.
God had multiplied Israel as the stars of heaven, fulfilling His promise to Abraham. Their great number was itself a blessing.
Moses breaks into a prayer: may God multiply them a thousand times more! His love for his people shines through.
Yet how could one man carry all their troubles, burdens, and disputes?
So Moses asked the people to choose wise, discerning, respected men from each tribe to serve as leaders.
The people agreed it was a good plan. Shared leadership was a joint decision.
Moses appointed these leaders over groups of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens — a system of delegation first suggested by Jethro.
Moses charged the judges to listen fairly and judge righteously, including cases involving foreigners.
Judges must not show favoritism or fear powerful people, because justice belongs to God. Hard cases could come to Moses. A timeless standard for anyone who judges.
Moses taught them everything they needed to do.
From Horeb they traveled through the great, frightening wilderness to Kadesh-barnea, at the southern edge of Canaan.
At Kadesh Moses told them they had arrived at the land God was giving them.
“Go up and possess it… fear not, neither be discouraged.” God’s invitation came with encouragement.
Here Deuteronomy adds a detail: the people themselves proposed sending spies first. Numbers 13 records that the Lord then approved the plan.

f.w: We will send men before us

chapters.n: Moses agreed and chose twelve men, one per tribe.
They went into the hill country and explored the valley of Eshcol.

f.g: “Valley of the cluster,” named for the huge grape cluster found there (Numbers 13:23-24).

chapters.n: They brought back fruit and reported: it is a good land God is giving us.
But the people refused to go — rebelling against God’s command.
They grumbled in their tents that God hated them and brought them out of Egypt only to destroy them — a terrible misreading of His love.
They complained the spies had frightened them: the people were bigger, the cities walled to the sky, and the giant Anakim lived there.

f.g: Anakim — a people known for great height (Numbers 13:33).

chapters.n: Moses had pleaded with them not to be afraid.
The Lord goes before you and will fight for you, just as you saw Him do in Egypt.
In the wilderness God carried them like a father carries his son. A tender image of God’s care through every step.

f.w: as a man doth bear his son

chapters.n: Yet despite all this, they did not trust the Lord.
He had gone before them, finding campsites and guiding them by fire at night and cloud by day. Their unbelief came despite constant evidence.
The Lord heard their words, grew angry, and swore an oath.
Not one of that generation would see the good land.
Except Caleb, who wholly followed the Lord. He would receive the very land he had walked on — Hebron.
Moses notes that God was angry with him too “for your sakes” — linking his own exclusion to the people’s rebellion that provoked him at Meribah.

f.w: the LORD was angry with me

chapters.n: Joshua, Moses’ assistant, will lead Israel in. Moses is told to encourage him.
The children the people feared would become victims are the very ones who will inherit the land. God’s mercy rests on the innocent.

f.w: no knowledge between good and evil
f.g: Too young to be accountable — compare Moroni 8:10-12 on little children.

chapters.n: The adults were told to turn back into the wilderness toward the Red Sea.
Then, too late, the people confessed and decided to fight after all, arming themselves for battle.
God warned them not to go, because He would not be with them. Obedience at the wrong time is not obedience.
They would not listen and went up proudly into the hills.
The Amorites swarmed out like bees and chased them all the way to Hormah.

f.g: A vivid image of being chased by a furious swarm.

chapters.n: They returned weeping before the Lord, but He did not respond. Tears after rebellion did not undo its consequences.
So they stayed at Kadesh a long time.
After the defeat at Hormah, Israel turned back into the wilderness as God had said and circled the mountains of Seir for many years — the long wandering.

f.g: The rugged mountain country of Edom, south of the Dead Sea.

chapters.n: Then, after many years, the Lord spoke again.
“You have circled this mountain long enough: turn north.” The time of waiting was over.
Israel would pass by the land of Esau’s descendants, who would be afraid. God warns Israel to be careful not to take advantage of that fear.

f.w: your brethren the children of Esau

chapters.n: Do not provoke them, for God gave Mount Seir to Esau. God keeps His promises to other nations too, not only to Israel.

f.g: Do not provoke or start a fight.

f.w: I have given mount Seir unto Esau

chapters.n: Israel is to pay honestly for food and water — no taking by force.

f.g: In KJV English, food in general.

chapters.n: They can afford it, because God has blessed their work and been with them all forty years. They lacked nothing. A beautiful summary of God’s quiet daily care.

f.g: He has watched over your journey.

chapters.n: They passed Edom by way of the Arabah road from Elath and Ezion-gaber, then turned toward the wilderness of Moab.

f.g: A port at the northern tip of the Gulf of Aqaba, near Ezion-gaber.
The Arabah, the rift valley south of the Dead Sea.

chapters.n: God also told them not to harass Moab, because He had given Ar to Lot’s descendants.

f.g: A Moabite city or region; here it stands for Moab’s land.

chapters.n: A historical note follows (verses 10–12): Moab had once been inhabited by the Emim, a large, tall people.

f.g: Emim — perhaps “terrors”; an early people of the region (Genesis 14:5).

chapters.n: Like the Anakim, they were considered giants — the Moabites called them Emim.
The Horites once lived in Seir before Esau’s descendants displaced them. The point: God gives lands to peoples, as He was giving Canaan to Israel.
Moses resumes: God told them to cross the brook Zered, Moab’s southern border, and they did.
It had been thirty-eight years since Kadesh-barnea. By then the generation of soldiers who refused to enter had died, exactly as God had sworn.
The Lord’s hand was against them until they were all gone. God’s word, even His warnings, never fails.
When the last of those warriors had died,
the Lord spoke to Moses again. A new chapter begins with a new generation.
Israel was now to pass by Ar on Moab’s border.
Approaching Ammon, they must not provoke them either, for God gave Ammon to Lot’s descendants as well.
Another historical aside (verses 20–23): Ammon’s land had also once belonged to giants, whom the Ammonites called Zamzummim.

f.g: Zamzummim — an early people, possibly the same as the Zuzim of Genesis 14:5.

chapters.n: They were tall like the Anakim, but the Lord destroyed them before the Ammonites, who settled in their place.
Just as He did for Esau’s descendants against the Horites. If God could do this for these nations, He could surely do it for Israel.
The Avim, who lived in villages as far as Gaza, were displaced by the Caphtorim — likely the Philistines, who came from Caphtor (Crete).

f.g: Usually identified with Crete; the Philistines came from there (Amos 9:7).

chapters.n: Now God commands them to cross the Arnon and take on Sihon, king of Heshbon. Unlike Edom, Moab, and Ammon, the Amorites’ land is part of Israel’s inheritance.
From now on, nations who hear of Israel will be filled with dread — as Rahab in Jericho later confirmed.
Even so, Moses first sent messengers with an offer of peace to Sihon. Israel tried peace before war.

f.g: A desert area east of Moab, later a Levite city (Joshua 13:18).

chapters.n: “Let me pass through on the main road; I won’t turn aside.”

f.g: The main road, probably the King’s Highway.

chapters.n: Israel offered to pay for food and water, just walking through.
As Edom and Moab had allowed — at least selling them supplies — until Israel crossed the Jordan.
Sihon refused. The text says God hardened his spirit — a way of saying God allowed Sihon’s own stubbornness to bring the consequences that delivered him into Israel’s hands.
The Lord said He had begun to give Sihon’s land to Israel: begin to take possession.
Sihon and his army came out to fight at Jahaz.
The Lord gave Israel victory over Sihon, his sons, and his people.
Israel captured his towns and devoted them to destruction, leaving no survivors. This hard practice (ḥerem) is described in the book as God’s judgment on the Amorites’ long wickedness.

f.g: Hebrew ḥaram — to devote wholly to God, usually by destruction.

chapters.n: They kept only the livestock and plunder.
From Aroer on the Arnon gorge to Gilead, no city was too strong, for the Lord gave them all. The very walls that had once frightened Israel’s parents fell easily.

f.w: there was not one city too strong for us

chapters.n: Israel did not touch Ammon’s land, the upper Jabbok, or anything God had forbidden. Their obedience covered both what to take and what to leave alone.
Next Israel turned north toward Bashan, and King Og came out to fight at Edrei.

f.g: A fertile plateau east of the Sea of Galilee.

chapters.n: The Lord told Moses not to fear, for He would give Og into their hands like Sihon.
The Lord delivered Og and his people completely.
Israel captured all sixty cities of the region of Argob, Og’s kingdom.

f.g: A district within Bashan, perhaps meaning “stony.”

chapters.n: These were fortified cities with high walls, gates, and bars, plus many unwalled villages. The fortresses the spies had feared proved no match for God.

f.g: Heavy beams used to bolt city gates.

chapters.n: They devoted these cities to destruction as they had with Sihon.

f.g: Devoted wholly to God (ḥerem), usually by destruction.

chapters.n: The livestock and goods were kept as plunder.
Israel now held the land east of the Jordan from the Arnon River up to Mount Hermon.

f.g: The tall, snow-capped mountain at Israel’s far north (about 9,200 feet).

chapters.n: A note on names: the Sidonians called Hermon “Sirion,” and the Amorites “Shenir.”
This included the plateau towns, all of Gilead, and all of Bashan.

f.g: The high tableland (mishor) north of the Arnon.

chapters.n: Og was the last of the Rephaim, an ancient race of giants. His huge iron (or basalt) bed — about 13 feet long and 6 feet wide — was still displayed in Rabbah of Ammon.

f.g: Hebrew Rephaim — an ancient people remembered for great size.
Possibly a bed of dark basalt, which looks like iron, or a coffin-like couch.
Rabbah, capital of Ammon — modern Amman, Jordan.

chapters.n: Moses gave the land from Aroer to half of Gilead to Reuben and Gad.
The rest of Gilead and all of Bashan went to the half tribe of Manasseh.
Jair of Manasseh took the Argob region and named its villages after himself, Havvoth-jair.

f.g: Small Aramean kingdoms north of Bashan.

chapters.n: Gilead was given to Machir, the Manassite clan that had conquered it (Numbers 32:39-40).
Reuben and Gad received the land from Gilead to the Arnon and up to the Jabbok, Ammon’s border.
Also the Jordan valley from the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea, below the slopes of Pisgah.
Moses reminded these tribes that, though they had their land, their fighting men must cross over armed with their brothers.

f.w: pass over armed before your brethren

chapters.n: Their families and herds could stay in the eastern cities.
Only after the Lord gave rest to all Israel west of the Jordan could they return home. Brotherhood meant finishing the work together.

f.g: Peace and security in the land.

chapters.n: Moses encouraged Joshua: you have seen what God did to these two kings; He will do the same to every kingdom you face.
Do not fear them, for the Lord Himself fights for you.
Moses now shares a personal moment: he pleaded with the Lord.
He praised God: You have only begun to show me Your greatness. What god in heaven or earth can do such works?

f.w: what God is there in heaven or in earth

chapters.n: Moses asked to cross over and see the good land — “that goodly mountain” and Lebanon. After forty years of leading, he longed to finish the journey.

f.g: The fine hill country of Canaan.

chapters.n: But the Lord, angry “for your sakes,” said, “Enough — speak no more of this.” Even a great prophet received a “no” to a heartfelt prayer.
Instead, God let Moses climb Pisgah and view the land in every direction. A gift within the disappointment.
Moses must charge, encourage, and strengthen Joshua, who would lead Israel in. Moses’ last work was preparing his successor.
So Israel stayed in the valley across from Beth-peor — the place of their recent sin, and where Moses would later be buried.
Having reviewed history, Moses turns to its lesson: listen and obey God’s statutes so you may live and enter the land. History is retold to lead to obedience.
Do not add to God’s word or take away from it. People must not alter what God has said — though God Himself may continue to reveal more, as He did after Moses.

f.w: Ye shall not add unto the word

chapters.n: They had just seen what happened at Baal-peor: those who followed that false god were destroyed.
But all who held tightly to the Lord are still alive. Faithfulness and life are linked.
Moses has taught them God’s laws, as commanded, to live by in the new land.
Keeping these laws will be Israel’s wisdom before the world. Other nations will notice and say, “What a wise people!” Obedience becomes a witness.

f.w: this is your wisdom and your understanding

chapters.n: What other nation has a God so near, who answers whenever they call? Israel’s true greatness lay in His closeness.
And what nation has laws as righteous as these?
Guard your soul carefully so you never forget what you have seen — and teach it to your children and grandchildren. Faith must be passed on deliberately.

f.w: teach them thy sons, and thy sons' sons

chapters.n: Especially remember Horeb, when God gathered the people to hear His words so they would reverence Him and teach their children.

f.g: Reverence and respect Me — awe more than terror.

chapters.n: They stood at the foot of the mountain as it blazed with fire into the sky, wrapped in dark clouds.
The Lord spoke from the fire. They heard His voice but saw no form. This mattered: they had no image of God to copy into an idol.

f.g: Saw no shape or form. Latter-day Saints believe God has a glorified form, but the people that day only heard His voice (compare Exodus 24:10; Moses 1:2).

chapters.n: He declared His covenant, the Ten Commandments, and wrote them on two stone tablets.
God also told Moses to teach them more detailed laws for life in the land.
Since they saw no form at Horeb, they must be careful...
...not to corrupt themselves by making an idol in the shape of a man or woman...
…or any animal on the ground or any bird in the sky, as Egypt’s animal-headed gods were pictured…
...or any creeping thing or fish. Every part of creation was off-limits as an object of worship — the Creator alone deserves it.
Nor should they worship the sun, moon, and stars, which God gave as lights for all nations. Worshiping created things instead of the Creator was common in the ancient world.

f.g: Allotted to all peoples as lights (Genesis 1:14-18).

chapters.n: God rescued Israel from Egypt, an “iron furnace” of suffering, to be His treasured people. Their identity rests on His rescue.

f.g: A smelting furnace — an image of intense affliction (1 Kings 8:51; 1 Nephi 20:10).

chapters.n: Moses repeats that God, angry with him on their account, swore he would not enter the land.
He must die here east of the Jordan; they will go over. Moses speaks without bitterness, focused on their future.
Be careful not to forget God’s covenant by making any image He has forbidden.
For the Lord is “a consuming fire, a jealous God” — His holiness burns away evil, and His love will not share His people with false gods.

f.g: Zealous to protect an exclusive covenant love (Exodus 34:14).

chapters.n: Moses looks ahead: after generations in the land, they may grow comfortable, make idols, and provoke God.
He calls heaven and earth as witnesses: if they do this, they will lose the land quickly.

f.w: I call heaven and earth to witness

chapters.n: The Lord will scatter them among the nations, few in number. This came true with the Assyrian and Babylonian exiles — and the Book of Mormon speaks of Israel’s scattering and gathering.
There they would serve man-made gods of wood and stone that cannot see, hear, eat, or smell — a tragic irony for people who had heard the living God speak.
Yet a promise of hope: even in exile, if they seek the Lord with all their heart and soul, they will find Him.
In the “latter days,” in their distress, if they turn back and obey, He will receive them. Latter-day Saints see this fulfilled in the ongoing gathering of Israel.
For the Lord is merciful. He will not abandon them or forget His covenant with their fathers.

f.w: the LORD thy God is a merciful God

chapters.n: Moses invites them to search all history and all the world: has anything like this ever happened?
Has any people heard God speak from fire and lived?
Has any god ever taken a nation out from another by miracles, plagues, war, and power, as the Lord did in Egypt?

f.g: Trials or tests — here the plagues that tested Egypt.

chapters.n: All this was shown so they would know the Lord is God and there is no other.

f.w: there is none else beside him

chapters.n: From heaven He spoke to teach them; on earth He showed them His great fire.
Why did God do it? Because He loved their fathers and chose their descendants. Election flows from love, not merit.
To drive out stronger nations and give Israel their land.
So know it and take it to heart: the Lord is God in heaven and on earth. There is no other.
Therefore keep His commandments, so it will go well with you and your children forever in the land. Obedience is presented as the path to lasting blessing.

f.w: that it may go well with thee

chapters.n: Now the narrator reports that Moses set apart three cities of refuge east of the Jordan, as commanded in Numbers.
These were for someone who killed a neighbor accidentally, without prior hatred, so that he could flee there and live.
Bezer for Reuben, Ramoth in Gilead for Gad, and Golan in Bashan for Manasseh — one in each eastern territory.

f.g: A city that later figured in several wars (1 Kings 22:3).

chapters.n: Verses 44–49 introduce Moses’ second and main address, the law itself (chapters 5–26).
These are the testimonies, statutes, and judgments he spoke after the Exodus.

f.g: Solemn covenant requirements, God’s witnessed decrees.

chapters.n: He spoke them east of the Jordan, near Beth-peor, in the land once ruled by Sihon.
Israel had taken the lands of Sihon and Og, the two Amorite kings east of the Jordan.
From Aroer by the Arnon up to Mount Sion — another name for Hermon (not the Zion of Jerusalem).

f.g: Here a name for Mount Hermon, spelled differently in Hebrew from Zion in Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Including the Jordan valley down to the Dead Sea, below the slopes of Pisgah.

f.g: The Dead Sea, at the south of the Arabah valley.

chapters.n: Moses gathers all Israel and calls them to hear, learn, keep, and do God’s laws. Four verbs: listening must lead to living.
The Lord made a covenant with Israel at Horeb (Sinai).

f.g: A sacred, two-way agreement between God and His people.

chapters.n: Many listening were children or not yet born at Sinai, yet Moses says the covenant was made “with us, who are all of us here alive.” Each generation must make the covenant its own.
The Lord spoke with them “face to face” from the fire — directly and personally, not through rumor.

f.g: Directly, personally; compare Moses’ unique closeness to God (Exodus 33:11; Moses 1:2).

chapters.n: Moses stood between God and the people because they were afraid of the fire. He was a mediator — a role ultimately fulfilled by Christ.

f.w: I stood between the LORD and you

chapters.n: The Ten Commandments begin with who God is and what He has done: “I am the LORD thy God, who freed you from slavery.” His laws flow from His saving love.

f.w: I am the LORD thy God

chapters.n: First: no other gods before Him. God must come first in our hearts.
Second: make no idols — carved images of anything in heaven, earth, or sea.

f.w: Thou shalt not make thee any graven image

chapters.n: Do not bow to or serve them. God is “jealous” — fiercely protective of His covenant. The consequences of hating God can echo through generations, as children learn sins from their parents.

f.g: Zealous for an exclusive covenant relationship.

f.w: visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children

chapters.n: But His mercy reaches thousands of generations of those who love Him. Mercy vastly outweighs judgment.
Third: do not take God’s name in vain — don’t use it carelessly, falsely, or for empty oaths. Honoring His name includes honoring the covenants made in it.

f.w: Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain

chapters.n: Fourth: keep the Sabbath holy. Exodus says “remember”; Deuteronomy says “keep” — guard it.
Six days are for work. The Sabbath does not despise labor; it sets it within a holy rhythm.
The seventh day is the Lord’s; no one works — not children, servants, animals, or foreigners. Deuteronomy adds: so your servants can rest just like you. The Sabbath is a gift of rest for everyone.

f.w: that thy manservant and thy maidservant may rest as well as thou
f.g: A detail unique to Deuteronomy’s version, stressing compassion.

chapters.n: Here is a key difference from Exodus: there the Sabbath recalls creation; here it recalls deliverance from slavery. Rest is a celebration of freedom God gave.

f.w: remember that thou wast a servant

f.g: An image of God’s powerful intervention.

chapters.n: Fifth: honor your father and mother, with the promise of long life and blessing in the land. Paul called this “the first commandment with promise.”

f.w: Honour thy father and thy mother

chapters.n: Sixth: do not kill — meaning murder, the unlawful taking of life. Jesus extended it to anger in the heart.
Seventh: do not commit adultery. Jesus taught that purity begins in the thoughts.
Eighth: do not steal. Respecting others’ property is part of loving your neighbor.
Ninth: do not give false testimony against your neighbor — no lying that harms others.
Tenth: do not covet what belongs to others. Deuteronomy lists the neighbor’s wife first and separately, and adds “his field.” This last command reaches inside the heart, where the other sins begin.

f.g: Desire wrongfully what belongs to someone else.

f.w: Neither shalt thou desire thy neighbour's wife

chapters.n: God spoke these ten words with a great voice from the fire and cloud — and added no more. He wrote them on two stone tablets and gave them to Moses.

f.g: These ten were spoken directly to all the people; other laws came through Moses.

chapters.n: Hearing God’s voice from the burning mountain, the tribal leaders and elders came to Moses.
They said, “We have seen God’s glory and heard His voice — God can speak with man and the man lives!”

f.w: God doth talk with man, and he liveth

chapters.n: But fear overcame them: if they heard more, they thought, the fire would consume them.
Who has ever heard the living God from the fire and lived?
They asked Moses to go near, listen, and tell them what God said — promising to hear and obey. They chose a mediator instead of direct experience.
The Lord heard and said their request was good.
Then a heartfelt longing from God Himself: “Oh, that they had such a heart, to always reverence Me and keep My commandments, so it would go well with them forever!” God desires our happiness.

f.w: O that there were such an heart in them

chapters.n: God told Moses to send the people back to their tents.
But Moses was to stay by God and receive all the laws to teach them. This is why Moses now teaches these laws in Deuteronomy.
Be careful to do as God commanded — turning neither right nor left. Stay on the path.

f.w: not turn aside to the right hand or to the left

chapters.n: Walk in all His ways, so you may live, prosper, and remain long in the land. God’s commandments lead to life.
Moses introduces the commandments God told him to teach, to be lived in the promised land.
The goal: that Israel would reverence the Lord and keep His commandments across generations — parent, child, and grandchild — and live long.

f.g: Reverence, awe, and loyal respect for God.

chapters.n: Listen and obey, so you may prosper and grow in the land “flowing with milk and honey.”

f.g: A picture of abundance: rich pasture for herds and plentiful food.

chapters.n: This is the Shema (“Hear”), the central confession of Judaism, recited daily: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD.” It declares that Israel worships one God alone. Latter-day Saints understand this oneness to include perfect unity of purpose among the Godhead.

f.g: Hebrew echad — one, unique, alone. See also John 17:21-22 and 3 Nephi 11:27 on divine unity.

chapters.n: Love God with all your heart, soul, and might — with everything you are. Jesus called this the first and great commandment.

f.w: thou shalt love the LORD thy God

chapters.n: God’s words must be written on the heart, not just on stone. Obedience starts inside.
Teach them diligently to your children — talk about them at home, on the road, at bedtime, and in the morning. Gospel teaching belongs in everyday life.

f.w: teach them diligently unto thy children

chapters.n: Bind them on your hand and between your eyes: let God’s word guide what you do and what you see. Many Jews fulfill this literally with tefillin — small boxes containing scripture.

f.g: Bands worn on the forehead; in Jewish practice, tefillin (phylacteries).

chapters.n: Write them on your doorposts and gates. Jewish homes still attach a small case called a mezuzah to the doorframe with these words inside.

f.g: Hebrew mezuzot — doorposts; the source of the mezuzah tradition.

chapters.n: When God brings them into the land, He will give them great cities they did not build.
Houses already full, wells already dug, vineyards and olive groves already planted — blessings they did not earn. And they will eat until full.
Then comes the danger: forgetting the Lord who rescued them. Prosperity can be more spiritually dangerous than hardship.

f.w: beware lest thou forget the LORD

chapters.n: Reverence the Lord, serve Him, and swear oaths by His name only. Jesus quoted this verse to resist Satan’s temptation.

f.w: Thou shalt fear the LORD thy God, and serve him

chapters.n: Do not follow the gods of surrounding nations.
The Lord is jealous for His people and will not tolerate rivals; turning away would bring destruction.
Do not test the Lord as at Massah, where they demanded water and asked, “Is the LORD among us or not?” Jesus also quoted this to Satan.

f.g: Test, put to the test, try to force God’s hand.

f.w: as ye tempted him in Massah

chapters.n: Carefully keep His commandments, testimonies, and statutes.
Do what is right and good in the Lord’s sight, so all will go well and you may possess the good land.

f.w: right and good in the sight of the LORD

chapters.n: God will drive out their enemies as He promised.
Someday your child will ask: “What do all these laws mean?” Expect the question — and be ready.
Answer with your family’s story: We were slaves in Egypt, and the Lord brought us out with a mighty hand. The answer to “why obey?” begins with “what God did for us.”
Tell how the Lord sent great and terrible signs against Egypt, Pharaoh, and his household before our very eyes.
He brought us out in order to bring us in — freedom from something and freedom for something.

f.w: he brought us out from thence, that he might bring us in
f.g: A key pattern: deliverance leads to inheritance.

chapters.n: God gave these laws for our good always, to keep us alive. His commandments are expressions of His love, not arbitrary rules.
Faithful obedience will be counted as our righteousness before the Lord. Paul later taught that true righteousness ultimately comes through faith in Christ.
When God brings Israel into the land, He will drive out seven nations, each larger and stronger than Israel. Their names show the many peoples living in Canaan.

f.g: The inhabitants of Jerusalem before David captured it (2 Samuel 5:6-7).

chapters.n: Israel is to devote them to destruction and make no treaties with them. This hard command is presented as judgment on deep wickedness and as protection against Israel being drawn into it.

f.g: Hebrew ḥaram — devote wholly to God, usually by destruction.

chapters.n: No intermarriage with them — neither giving daughters nor taking wives.

f.w: Neither shalt thou make marriages with them

chapters.n: The reason is spiritual, not ethnic: such marriages would turn Israel’s children to other gods. Solomon’s life later proved the danger.

f.w: they will turn away thy son from following me

chapters.n: Destroy their altars, smash their sacred pillars, cut down their Asherah poles, and burn their idols. Remove every source of temptation.

f.g: Hebrew asherim — wooden poles honoring the goddess Asherah, not literal groves of trees.
Standing stone pillars used in pagan worship.

chapters.n: Why? Because Israel is a holy people, chosen by God as His treasured possession. To be chosen is to be set apart for a purpose.

f.g: Hebrew segullah — a treasured personal possession.

chapters.n: God did not choose Israel because they were many — they were the fewest of all peoples. Being chosen is not a reward for greatness.

f.w: ye were the fewest of all people

chapters.n: He chose them simply because He loved them and was keeping His oath to their fathers. Love and covenant faithfulness are the root of everything.
Know that the Lord is the faithful God, keeping covenant and mercy for a thousand generations with those who love Him and keep His commandments.
But He repays those who hate Him directly, “to their face” — personally and without delay.
So keep the commandments taught today.
If Israel listens and obeys, God will keep His covenant of loyal love sworn to their fathers.
He will love, bless, and multiply them — children, crops, grain, wine, oil, cattle, and flocks. Blessings touch every part of life.
They will be blessed above all peoples; no one, human or animal, will be barren.

f.g: Unable to have children or offspring.

chapters.n: God will protect them from sickness, including the terrible diseases they knew in Egypt.
Israel must not pity these nations or serve their gods, which would be a snare — a trap that catches the unwary.
If you wonder, “These nations are too many — how can we drive them out?”...

f.g: Drive out and take possession from.

chapters.n: ...don’t be afraid. Remember what God did to Pharaoh and Egypt. Remembering past deliverance builds present courage.
The plagues, signs, wonders, and mighty power you saw — God will do the same to every people you fear.
God will send “the hornet” against them, until even those hiding are gone. This may mean literal insects or a vivid image of panic and terror God sends ahead.
Don’t be terrified, for the Lord your God, great and awesome, is among you.
God will drive them out gradually, little by little, so the land doesn’t become wild and overrun by animals. God’s timing is wise even when it seems slow.
Yet He will certainly give them victory and throw their enemies into confusion.
Their kings will fall, and no one will be able to stand against Israel.

f.w: there shall no man be able to stand before thee

chapters.n: Burn their idols — and don’t keep the silver or gold on them. Greed for an idol’s gold can become its own trap, as Achan learned at Jericho.

f.w: thou shalt not desire the silver or gold

chapters.n: Don’t bring an idol into your home, or you too will become “devoted to destruction” like it. Utterly reject it. What we welcome into our homes shapes us.
Keep all the commandments so you may live, grow, and possess the land promised to your fathers.
Remember the whole forty-year journey. God used it to humble and test them, to reveal what was truly in their hearts. Trials show us who we are.

f.w: to know what was in thine heart

chapters.n: God let them hunger, then fed them manna — a food no one had known — to teach that people live not by bread alone, but by every word from God’s mouth. Jesus quoted this when tempted in the wilderness.

f.w: man doth not live by bread only

chapters.n: For forty years their clothes didn’t wear out and their feet didn’t swell. Quiet, daily miracles that are easy to overlook.
Like a loving father disciplines his son, the Lord disciplines Israel. Hardship was training, not rejection.

f.w: as a man chasteneth his son

chapters.n: So keep God’s commandments, walk in His ways, and reverence Him.
God is bringing them into a good land — full of streams, springs, and deep waters. After decades in dry desert, this would sound like paradise.
A land of wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olive oil, and honey — the famous “seven species” still associated with the land of Israel.

f.g: Probably date syrup as well as bees’ honey.

chapters.n: There they will lack nothing; even the rocks hold iron, and the hills hold copper to mine.
When you have eaten and are full, bless the Lord for the good land. Jewish families still use this verse as the basis for the blessing after meals.
Beware of forgetting the Lord — and forgetting Him shows up as neglecting His commandments.
The danger comes after you have eaten well, built fine houses, and settled in.
When herds, flocks, silver, gold, and everything else multiply...
...then your heart becomes proud and you forget the God who freed you. The Book of Mormon calls this the “pride cycle.”
Remember who led you through that great and terrible wilderness, with venomous snakes, scorpions, and drought — and brought water out of hard rock.
He fed you manna to humble and test you — so He could do you good in the end. God’s training aims at our ultimate blessing.

f.w: to do thee good at thy latter end
f.g: To bless you in the end.

chapters.n: The great temptation: to say, “My own strength and skill earned me this wealth.”

f.w: My power and the might of mine hand

chapters.n: Remember, it is God who gives the ability to gain wealth — in order to fulfill His covenant. Our talents and opportunities are His gifts.

f.w: he that giveth thee power to get wealth

chapters.n: If you forget the Lord and serve other gods, Moses solemnly warns, you will surely perish.

f.g: I solemnly warn you, as a witness.

chapters.n: Like the nations God is driving out, so would Israel perish if they disobeyed. Israel’s covenant gave them no exemption from God’s justice.
“Hear, O Israel”: you are about to cross the Jordan to face nations stronger than you, with cities fortified “up to heaven.”

f.g: With very high walls — an exaggeration for effect, echoing the spies’ fearful report (1:28).

chapters.n: Including the tall Anakim, famous in a proverb: “Who can stand before the sons of Anak?”
But understand: the Lord goes ahead of you like a consuming fire and will bring them down. Victory belongs to Him.
After victory, don’t say, “God gave us this land because we’re so righteous.” It is because of those nations’ wickedness.
Not for your goodness, but because of their wickedness — and because God keeps His promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Compare Nephi’s similar teaching about why the Canaanites were driven out.

f.w: for the wickedness of these nations

chapters.n: Understand clearly: you receive this land despite being stiff-necked. Grace, not merit, gives the inheritance.

f.g: Stubborn, like an ox that will not bend its neck to the yoke.

chapters.n: Remember — never forget — how you provoked God from the day you left Egypt until now. Moses now recalls their worst moment as proof.
Even at Horeb, while the covenant was being made, they provoked God so much He was ready to destroy them.
Moses spent forty days and nights on the mountain receiving the covenant tablets, without food or water.
God gave him two stone tablets written “with the finger of God,” containing the words He had spoken from the fire.

f.g: The day all Israel gathered at Sinai.

chapters.n: At the end of the forty days, the Lord gave Moses the tablets of the covenant.
Then God told him to hurry down: the people had already corrupted themselves and made a metal idol. How quickly they turned aside!

f.g: An idol made of melted, cast metal.

chapters.n: God said, “I see that this is a stiff-necked people.”
“Let Me alone, so I can destroy them — and I will make a greater nation from you.” A test of Moses’ heart: would he accept personal glory or plead for the people?
Moses came down from the burning mountain, the tablets in his hands.
He saw the golden calf. They had turned aside so quickly.
He threw down the tablets and broke them before their eyes — a vivid picture that the covenant had been broken.
Moses fell before the Lord another forty days and nights, fasting, because of their sin. True intercession is costly.

f.w: I fell down before the LORD

chapters.n: He feared God’s burning anger — yet the Lord listened to him once again.

f.w: the LORD hearkened unto me at that time also

chapters.n: The Lord was angry enough with Aaron, who made the calf, to destroy him too — but Moses prayed for Aaron as well. This detail appears only here.
Moses took “your sin” — the calf — burned it, crushed it to dust, and threw the dust into the stream. Sin had to be utterly destroyed.
And the rebellion didn’t stop there: Taberah (fire), Massah (testing God), Kibroth-hattaavah (craving meat).
At Kadesh-barnea, when God said “Go up and possess the land,” they rebelled, did not believe, and did not listen.
Moses sums it up bluntly: “You have been rebellious since the day I knew you.” Honest memory guards against pride.
So Moses lay prostrate forty days and nights, because the Lord said He would destroy them.
Moses prays: “O Lord GOD, don’t destroy Your people, Your inheritance, whom You redeemed from Egypt.” He appeals to God’s own investment in them.

f.g: Your own possession — the people who belong to You.

chapters.n: “Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; don’t look at this people’s stubbornness and sin.” He pleads on the basis of the covenant, not the people’s merit.

f.w: Remember thy servants, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob

chapters.n: He also appeals to God’s reputation: Egypt would say the Lord couldn’t bring them in, or hated them.

f.w: Lest the land whence thou broughtest us out say

chapters.n: “They are Your people, whom You brought out with Your mighty power.” Moses’ intercession foreshadows Christ, who pleads for us not by our worthiness but by His own.

f.g: An image of God’s powerful deliverance.

chapters.n: Moses picks up the story after the golden calf. Even though Israel broke the covenant, the Lord invites Moses back up the mountain to start again with new stone tablets and a wooden chest to hold them.

f.w: Hew thee two tables of stone like unto the first

chapters.n: God promises to rewrite what was on the broken tablets. The covenant can be renewed — a pattern of second chances that runs through all of scripture.

f.w: I will write on the tables
f.g: JST adds that the second tablets lacked “the words of the everlasting covenant of the holy priesthood” (compare JST Exodus 34:1-2).

chapters.n: Moses obeys exactly: he builds the ark from acacia wood, cuts the tablets, and climbs the mountain carrying them.

f.g: Acacia, a hard, durable desert wood used for the tabernacle and its furniture.

chapters.n: The Lord himself writes the same Ten Commandments again — the words Israel had heard from the fire at Sinai when they gathered as a people.

f.g: The day Israel gathered at the foot of Sinai to hear God speak (Deuteronomy 9:10).

chapters.n: Moses places the tablets in the ark, where they were still kept as he spoke. The covenant was literally carried at the center of Israel’s camp.
A brief travel note interrupts Moses’ speech, reminding listeners that Aaron died on the journey and that the priesthood passed to his son Eleazar, so the work continued.
More stops on the wilderness route. Jotbath is remembered as a well-watered place, a small mercy in a dry land.

f.g: Probably the same as Hor-hagidgad in Numbers 33.

chapters.n: The Levites were set apart for three sacred jobs: carrying the ark, serving before the Lord at the sanctuary, and pronouncing blessings in his name.
Levi received no territory like the other tribes. Their “inheritance” was the Lord himself and the service of his house, supported by the people’s offerings.
Moses again spent forty days on the mountain, and his pleading on Israel’s behalf was heard. A prophet’s intercession turned away destruction.
Instead of ending the journey, God tells Moses to lead the people onward to the land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Forgiveness opens the way forward.

f.w: which I sware unto their fathers

chapters.n: Moses now turns to the heart of the matter: what does God actually want? Not mere ritual, but reverence, faithful living, love, and wholehearted service.

f.w: what doth the LORD thy God require of thee

f.g: “Fear” here means deep reverence and respect, not terror.

chapters.n: The commandments are given “for thy good.” God’s laws are not arbitrary burdens but a gift meant to bless those who keep them.
Everything — the earth and every layer of heaven — belongs to God. That makes his choice of Israel all the more striking.

f.g: A Hebrew way of saying “the highest heavens,” all of heaven together.

chapters.n: Out of all that he owns, the Lord set his love on the patriarchs and chose their descendants. Being chosen is a gift of grace and a call to responsibility.

f.w: he chose their seed after them

chapters.n: Circumcision was the outward sign of the covenant; Moses asks for the inward reality — a heart open and responsive to God instead of stubborn.

f.w: Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart

f.g: Stubborn, like an ox that will not bend its neck to the yoke.

chapters.n: God is supreme over every power. He is impartial and cannot be bribed — a direct contrast to corrupt human judges and to the gods of the nations.

f.w: God of gods, and Lord of lords

chapters.n: This mighty God personally defends orphans and widows and cares for foreigners. His greatness is shown in how he treats the vulnerable.
Israel must treat outsiders the way God treats them — remembering what it felt like to be foreigners and slaves in Egypt.
Four verbs sum up covenant loyalty: revere him, serve him, hold tight to him, and make your promises in his name alone.

f.g: Cleave = cling closely, the same word used of marriage in Genesis 2:24.

chapters.n: The Lord is the reason Israel can praise at all. They had personally witnessed his mighty acts in Egypt and the wilderness.
Jacob’s family went to Egypt as just seventy people; now they are a vast nation. God has already kept his promise to Abraham.
Love comes first, and obedience flows from it. Moses links loving God with keeping every part of his law, not just on special days but always.

f.g: Charge = the duties or responsibilities God has entrusted to you.

chapters.n: Moses speaks to the people who personally lived through these events as youths. They can’t claim ignorance; they have firsthand experience of God’s discipline and power.

f.g: Correction or training, the way a parent disciplines a child (Deuteronomy 8:5).

f.w: his mighty hand, and his stretched out arm

chapters.n: He lists what they saw: the signs and plagues that God sent against Pharaoh and the whole land of Egypt.
The great rescue at the Red Sea: the most powerful army of the day was swept away by the returning waters. Egypt’s chariot force never threatened Israel again.

f.w: the water of the Red sea to overflow them

chapters.n: God’s care did not stop at the sea. Through forty years of wilderness he fed, led, and corrected them until they reached the plains of Moab.

f.w: what he did unto you in the wilderness

chapters.n: A sobering memory: Dathan and Abiram rebelled against Moses’ leadership, and the earth opened and swallowed them. Rebellion against God’s appointed order has consequences.
The point of the list: “you saw it all yourselves.” Personal witness brings personal accountability.
Obedience is the source of strength. Keeping the commandments is what will make Israel able to enter and hold the land.
Long life in the land is tied to faithfulness. The land’s richness is pictured as flowing milk (from flocks) and honey (from bees or date syrup).

f.w: a land that floweth with milk and honey

chapters.n: In Egypt, crops depended on Nile irrigation; farmers moved water through channels, possibly opening and closing them with their feet or working foot-driven water wheels.

f.g: Likely refers to opening irrigation ditches with the foot or treading a water wheel.

chapters.n: Canaan is hilly, with no great river to rely on. Its life depends on rain — and so on God. This land would teach Israel daily trust.

f.w: drinketh water of the rain of heaven

chapters.n: A tender picture: God personally watches over this land all year long, from planting to harvest.

f.w: the eyes of the LORD thy God are always upon it

chapters.n: Here begins a passage later recited daily by Jews as part of the Shema prayer. The condition is wholehearted love and service.

f.w: with all your heart and with all your soul

chapters.n: Israel’s farming depended on two rainy seasons: the early rains of autumn that softened the ground for planting and the late rains of spring that filled out the grain.

f.w: the first rain and the latter rain

f.g: In KJV English, “corn” means grain such as wheat or barley.

chapters.n: God promises pasture for the animals and plenty for the people — blessings for the whole household.

f.w: that thou mayest eat and be full

chapters.n: The danger is subtle: a deceived heart. Prosperity can quietly lead people to trust other gods instead of the one who gave the blessings.

f.w: that your heart be not deceived

chapters.n: If Israel turned to idols, God would “shut up the heaven” — drought would follow. Elijah’s later drought fulfilled this warning.

f.w: he shut up the heaven, that there be no rain

chapters.n: God’s words must be stored inside and worn outside. Later Jews took the hand and forehead language literally with small leather boxes called tefillin.

f.g: Headbands or forehead markers; Jewish practice uses phylacteries (tefillin).

chapters.n: Parents are the first teachers. Gospel conversation belongs in everyday life — at home, on walks, at bedtime, and in the morning.

f.w: ye shall teach them your children

chapters.n: Writing God’s words on doorposts made every home a reminder of the covenant. Jewish homes still fix a small scroll, the mezuzah, to their doorframes.

f.g: Hebrew mezuzot; the source of the Jewish mezuzah.

chapters.n: The reward is a long, settled life in the land for generation after generation — “heaven on earth” for as long as the sky stands.

f.w: as the days of heaven upon the earth
f.g: An idiom for “as long as the heavens last” — permanently.

chapters.n: The conditions restated: diligent obedience, love, walking in God’s ways, and clinging to him.
With God fighting for them, Israel would overcome nations larger and stronger than itself.

f.w: greater nations and mightier than yourselves

chapters.n: The ideal borders of the promise stretch from the southern desert to Lebanon, and from the Euphrates to the Mediterranean. They were most nearly reached under David and Solomon.

f.w: Every place whereon the soles of your feet shall tread

f.g: In KJV English, “coast” means border or territory.

chapters.n: God would go ahead of them, filling their enemies with dread. Rahab later describes exactly this fear in Jericho.

f.w: the fear of you and the dread of you

chapters.n: Here is the great choice of Deuteronomy. God lays out two paths and lets Israel decide.
Blessing follows obedience. Agency is real, and so are its results.
The curse follows turning aside to follow gods they had never known — gods that had done nothing for them.

f.g: Gods with no history of saving Israel, unlike the Lord.

chapters.n: Once in the land, Israel was to hold a ceremony on two mountains facing each other near Shechem, declaring blessings from one and curses from the other.

f.w: mount Gerizim, and the curse upon mount Ebal

chapters.n: Moses gives directions: the mountains lie west of the Jordan in central Canaan, near the oaks of Moreh where Abraham first built an altar in the land.
A confident promise: they will cross the Jordan, take the land, and live there.
The section closes the way it began — with a call to careful obedience. This prepares for the detailed laws starting in chapter 12.

f.g: A Hebrew idiom: “be careful to do.”

chapters.n: This verse opens the long central law code of Deuteronomy (chapters 12–26). These are the rules for life in the promised land, meant to last as long as Israel lived there.

f.g: Statutes = fixed decrees; judgments = rulings for specific cases.

chapters.n: Canaanite worship sites were often on hilltops and under leafy trees, linked with fertility rituals. Israel must wipe out every one of them so idolatry would not take root.
Four kinds of pagan objects must go: altars, standing stones, sacred poles, and carved idols. Even the gods’ names were to be erased from the land.

f.g: Standing stones (Hebrew matsevot) used as cult symbols.
Hebrew asherim — wooden poles or trees honoring the goddess Asherah, not literal forests.

chapters.n: Israel must not worship the Lord the way the Canaanites worshiped their gods — at any hill, with any image, by any method they liked.

f.w: Ye shall not do so unto the LORD your God

chapters.n: God, not the people, would choose the place of central worship, where he would “put his name.” Over time this was the tabernacle at Shiloh and finally the temple in Jerusalem.
All the major offerings were to be brought to that one sanctuary: whole burnt offerings, other sacrifices, tithes, special contributions, promised gifts, voluntary gifts, and firstborn animals.

f.g: Portions lifted up or set apart as a gift to the Lord, often for the priests.
The first offspring of animals, which belonged to the Lord.

chapters.n: Worship was to be joyful. Families ate parts of their offerings together in God’s presence, celebrating his blessings on their work.
In the wilderness, practice had been somewhat loose. In the land, each person doing whatever seemed right would no longer be acceptable.

f.w: whatsoever is right in his own eyes

chapters.n: Israel had not yet reached its “rest” — the settled, secure life God promised. The full law of the central sanctuary waited for that day.
Once across the Jordan and secure from enemies, Israel would be able to live in peace and follow these rules fully.

f.w: he giveth you rest from all your enemies

chapters.n: The command repeated: one chosen place for the offerings. This unity of worship helped keep Israel united as one covenant people.

f.w: to cause his name to dwell there

chapters.n: Everyone shares in the celebration — children, servants, and the landless Levites. True worship includes those with less.

f.w: the Levite that is within your gates

chapters.n: Do not offer sacrifices at just any spot that looks appealing, as the Canaanites did.

f.w: in every place that thou seest
f.g: Any shrine or hilltop that seemed attractive.

chapters.n: Burnt offerings belong only at the place God chooses. Obedience in worship meant accepting God’s pattern, not inventing one’s own.

f.g: Eventually Jerusalem, in the territory of Benjamin and Judah.

chapters.n: Ordinary meat for food did not have to be a sacrifice. People could slaughter animals at home and eat them, clean or unclean in body alike, as they would eat wild game.

f.g: Lusteth = desires; here simply “whatever you want to eat.”

f.w: the roebuck, and as of the hart
f.g: Gazelle and deer — wild game that was never sacrificed.

chapters.n: One firm rule remained: never eat the blood. It was to be drained out and poured on the ground.

f.w: ye shall not eat the blood

chapters.n: Sacred portions — tithes, firstborn animals, vowed and freewill gifts — could not be eaten at home like regular meals.
These holy foods were eaten at the sanctuary in a joyful family feast that included servants and Levites.

f.g: At the sanctuary, in God’s presence.

chapters.n: The Levites depended on the generosity of others. Israel must never neglect them.
As Israel’s territory grew, people would live far from the sanctuary. Meat-eating at home is again permitted.
Distance from the sanctuary was no barrier to normal meals. They could slaughter from their herds at home, following the proper way.

f.g: This allowance replaced Leviticus 17:3-4, which required all slaughter at the tabernacle during the wilderness years.

chapters.n: Home-slaughtered meat was treated like game: anyone, ritually clean or not, could eat it.

f.g: People in either state of ritual purity, not clean or unclean animals.

chapters.n: The reason for the blood law: blood represents life, and life belongs to God. This reverence prepares for the atoning blood of Christ.
The rule is stated again for emphasis: pour the blood out like water.

f.w: pour it upon the earth as water

chapters.n: A third repetition, with a promise: obeying this will bring good to you and your descendants.

f.w: that it may go well with thee

chapters.n: Holy things and vows still had to go to the chosen place. The home-meat permission didn’t cover sacred gifts.
At the altar, burnt offerings were wholly consumed; for other sacrifices the blood went on the altar and the worshiper ate the meat.

f.w: the blood of thy sacrifices shall be poured out upon the altar

chapters.n: Moses urges careful listening and obedience so that blessings will continue for generations.

f.w: good and right in the sight of the LORD

chapters.n: After God removes the Canaanite nations, Israel will settle in their land.
A real danger: curiosity about how the previous inhabitants worshiped, leading Israel to copy them. Spiritual traps often begin with imitation.

f.g: Caught as in a hunter’s trap.

chapters.n: Canaanite religion included horrors like burning children as sacrifices. The Lord condemns such practices completely.

f.w: their sons and their daughters they have burnt in the fire

f.g: Something detestable and offensive to God.

chapters.n: God’s word must be kept whole — nothing added, nothing removed. (In Hebrew Bibles this verse begins chapter 13.)

f.w: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it

chapters.n: Moses addresses a hard case: someone claiming spiritual gifts — a prophet or a person who receives dreams — who backs up their message with a miraculous sign.
Even if the sign actually happens, the message itself is the test. Anyone urging Israel to follow other gods is false, no matter what wonders they perform.

f.w: the sign or the wonder come to pass

chapters.n: Signs alone do not prove truth. God allows such tests to reveal whether his people truly love him with their whole heart.

f.w: the LORD your God proveth you

chapters.n: Six strong verbs describe true discipleship: walk after him, revere him, keep his commandments, obey his voice, serve him, and cling to him.
Under the law of Moses, leading Israel into idolatry was treated as treason against the God who had freed them, and it carried the death penalty.

f.w: redeemed you out of the house of bondage
f.g: Redeem = to buy back or free a slave.

f.w: put the evil away from the midst of thee

chapters.n: The test gets personal: what if a sibling, child, spouse, or closest friend quietly tries to lead you toward other gods? Loyalty to God must come first.

f.w: which is as thine own soul
f.g: As dear to you as yourself.

chapters.n: It doesn’t matter whether those gods belong to neighbors close by or to distant lands — none of them are to be followed.

f.w: from the one end of the earth even unto the other end of the earth

chapters.n: No hiding it, no covering for them out of affection. Family ties could not shield someone trying to destroy the covenant community.

f.w: neither shall thine eye pity him

chapters.n: The witness who was enticed was to lead the execution, then the community joined in. This placed the gravest responsibility on the accuser.

f.w: thine hand shall be first upon him

chapters.n: Stoning was a public, communal punishment. Many later rabbis and modern readers note these laws were for ancient Israel’s theocratic setting; Jesus taught a higher law of mercy.

f.w: thou shalt stone him with stones

chapters.n: The punishment served as a deterrent: all Israel would hear and be warned away from such wickedness.

f.w: all Israel shall hear, and fear

chapters.n: A third case: rumors that an entire Israelite town has turned to idolatry.
Troublemakers have led the whole town astray to worship unknown gods.

f.g: Belial = worthlessness; “sons of Belial” means wicked, good-for-nothing men.

chapters.n: Before any action, the report must be carefully investigated. Justice requires certainty, not gossip.

f.w: inquire, and make search, and ask diligently

chapters.n: If it proves true, the town was to be treated like a Canaanite city under the ban — utterly destroyed.

f.g: Hebrew ḥerem — devoting something entirely to God by destruction.

chapters.n: Nothing could be kept as plunder. The whole city was burned as an offering to God and left as a permanent ruin.

f.g: Hebrew tel — a mound of ruins.

chapters.n: Keeping even a little of the devoted things would bring the curse on Israel — as Achan later learned. Purging evil makes room for God’s mercy and growth.
God’s compassion and blessing follow obedience — listening to his voice and doing what is right in his sight.

f.w: hearken to the voice of the LORD

chapters.n: Because Israel belongs to God as his children, they must not copy pagan mourning rituals like gashing the skin or shaving the front of the head for the dead.

f.g: Shaving the forehead as a mourning rite.

chapters.n: Israel is “holy” — set apart — and a “peculiar” people, meaning God’s own treasured possession. Their distinct way of life flows from that identity.

f.g: Hebrew segullah — a special treasure, not “odd.”

chapters.n: A summary rule introducing the food laws: do not eat anything God calls detestable.
Domestic animals that could be eaten: cattle, sheep, and goats — the main livestock of Israel.

f.w: These are the beasts which ye shall eat

chapters.n: Wild animals that could also be eaten. The exact identities of some of these Hebrew names are uncertain; they were various deer, gazelles, ibex, and antelopes.

f.g: Probably a kind of antelope or ibex; the Hebrew word is uncertain.
Likely a wild sheep; true chamois do not live in Israel.

chapters.n: The general rule for land animals: they must have a split hoof and chew the cud. Both signs were needed.

f.g: Brings up partly digested food to chew again, like cows and sheep.

chapters.n: Animals with only one of the two signs were off-limits — like the camel, hare, and rock badger, which appear to chew but lack a true split hoof.

f.g: The rock hyrax, a small rabbit-like animal living among rocks.
Rabbits move their jaws as if chewing cud, so they were classed this way.

chapters.n: The pig has a split hoof but does not chew the cud, so it was unclean — not to be eaten or even touched when dead.
Water creatures could be eaten if they had both fins and scales — like most ordinary fish.
Creatures without fins and scales — such as shellfish, eels, and catfish — were unclean.
Birds in general were allowed unless they were on the forbidden list that follows.

f.g: Such as doves, pigeons, quail, and chickens.

f.w: year by year in the place which the LORD shall choose

f.w: put the sickle to the corn

Remembering slavery in Egypt kept Israel humble and generous toward the vulnerable.

f.w: thou wast a bondman in Egypt

chapters.n: The third feast, Tabernacles, came in the fall after the grain and grapes were gathered. Families lived in leafy booths, recalling the wilderness years.
Again, the whole community rejoices — including those who might otherwise be left out.
A full week of celebration at the sanctuary, because God blesses the harvest and all their labor. Joy is commanded!
Three pilgrim feasts each year required the men to appear at the sanctuary, and none should come empty-handed.

f.w: they shall not appear before the LORD empty

chapters.n: Gifts were measured by ability and blessing, not a fixed price. God asks according to what we have.

chapters.n: Three rules for judges: don’t twist justice, don’t play favorites, and don’t accept bribes — because bribes blind even wise people.

chapters.n: “Justice, justice shall you pursue” — the Hebrew repeats the word for emphasis. Living in the land depended on a just society.

chapters.n: Nor any standing stone pillar used in Canaanite worship. The Lord hates such counterfeit worship.

f.g: Hebrew matsevah — a sacred standing stone.

chapters.n: Offering a sick or defective animal treated God with contempt. Sacrifices must be whole and the best one has.

f.g: Outside the city gate, the public place of judgment.

f.g: Deuteronomy’s usual phrase for the priests from the tribe of Levi.

chapters.n: Their verdict was binding. The people must follow it carefully.

chapters.n: Not swerving right or left — a common Deuteronomy image for complete obedience on a straight path.

f.w: to the right hand, nor to the left

chapters.n: Any king must be chosen by God and be a fellow Israelite, not a foreigner.

f.g: Greek Septuagint deuteronomion, “second law” — the source of the book’s name.

chapters.n: Moses now warns against the occult practices of Canaan. Israel must not learn them.

Trying to learn hidden things through omens or lots.
A fortune-teller or one who reads signs to find lucky days.

One who seeks to consult the dead.
