chapters.n: Ammonites and Moabites were barred from the assembly. Yet Ruth the Moabitess, through faith and conversion, became an ancestor of David and of Jesus.
The reason: they refused hospitality to Israel on the journey and even hired the seer Balaam to curse them.

f.g: A town near the Euphrates River.

chapters.n: God refused to curse Israel and turned Balaam’s words into blessings, simply because he loved them.

f.w: turned the curse into a blessing

chapters.n: Israel was not to make treaties seeking Ammon’s or Moab’s welfare — that is, no formal alliances.

f.g: Make a treaty or alliance with them.

chapters.n: Edomites were relatives — descendants of Jacob’s brother Esau. Egyptians had once hosted Israel. So these were not to be despised.
Their descendants could join the assembly after three generations.
An army camp must be morally and ritually clean, because God was present with the troops.

f.w: keep thee from every wicked thing

chapters.n: A man who had a nighttime emission was temporarily ritually unclean and stayed outside the camp.

f.w: uncleanness that chanceth him by night

chapters.n: By evening he washed and could return after sunset. Ritual impurity was not sin but required simple steps of cleansing.

f.g: The new day began at sunset.

chapters.n: A designated latrine area had to be set up outside the camp.
Each soldier carried a digging tool to bury waste — practical hygiene that protected health.

f.g: A digging tool or small spade.

chapters.n: The deeper reason: God walks among his people. A clean camp honored his presence. Latter-day Saints see a similar principle in keeping temples and lives clean.

f.w: the LORD thy God walketh in the midst of thy camp

chapters.n: A remarkable law: an escaped slave from another land must not be sent back to his master. Israel was to be a refuge.

f.g: Likely a slave fleeing from a foreign country.

chapters.n: He could live freely in any town he chose, and no one was to mistreat him.
No Israelite, man or woman, was to serve as a cult prostitute, a common feature of Canaanite fertility religion.

f.g: Hebrew qedeshah — a woman associated with pagan shrine prostitution.
Hebrew qadesh — a male shrine prostitute.

chapters.n: Earnings from prostitution could never be given as an offering to God. Money gained through sin cannot buy holiness.

f.g: Probably a crude term for a male prostitute’s wages.

chapters.n: Israelites must not charge interest to one another on loans of money, food, or anything else. Loans to the needy were acts of mercy, not profit.

f.g: In KJV, any interest on a loan, not just excessive interest.

chapters.n: Interest could be charged to foreign traders doing business, but not to fellow Israelites. Generosity brings God’s blessing.

f.w: Unto a stranger thou mayest lend upon usury
f.g: Here “stranger” means a foreigner (nokri), not a resident alien.

chapters.n: A vow to God must be kept promptly. Broken promises to God are sin.

f.w: thou shalt not slack to pay it

chapters.n: No one had to make vows; refraining was no sin. But once made, a vow was binding.
Whatever comes out of your mouth as a promise to God, do it. Integrity in speech matters.

f.w: That which is gone out of thy lips

chapters.n: A traveler could eat grapes in a neighbor’s vineyard to satisfy hunger, but not fill a basket to carry away.

f.w: thou shalt not put any in thy vessel
f.g: No harvesting for yourself — only eating on the spot.

chapters.n: Likewise, hungry passersby could pick grain by hand but not use a sickle. Jesus’ disciples did exactly this.

f.w: pluck the ears with thine hand

f.g: Unharvested grain still in the field.

chapters.n: Divorce existed in Israel, but it required a written certificate. The document protected the woman by proving she was free to remarry. Jesus later said Moses allowed this because of hardened hearts.

f.g: Hebrew “a matter of nakedness” — something shameful; its meaning was debated by later rabbis.

chapters.n: Once divorced, she was legally free to marry someone else.
If the second marriage also ended, by divorce or death…
…the first husband could not take her back. This rule likely discouraged hasty divorces and treating wives as exchangeable.

f.g: After she has been joined to another man.

chapters.n: A newlywed husband was excused from military service and public duties for a full year so he could build a happy marriage. God cares about joy in marriage.
A lender couldn’t take a family’s millstone as collateral, because without it they couldn’t grind grain for daily bread.

f.w: the nether or the upper millstone
f.g: The lower or upper stone of a hand mill.

chapters.n: Kidnapping a fellow Israelite to enslave or sell him was a capital crime — as Joseph’s brothers had done to him.

f.g: Treats him as goods to sell.

chapters.n: For serious skin diseases, the people must carefully follow the priests’ instructions given in Leviticus.

f.g: Various skin diseases, not only modern leprosy.

chapters.n: Remember Miriam: when she spoke against Moses, she was struck with this disease and shut outside the camp for seven days.
A lender couldn’t barge into a borrower’s home to seize collateral, protecting the poor person’s dignity and privacy.

f.g: To take the security for the loan.

chapters.n: The lender must wait outside and let the borrower bring out what he chose.
If a poor man gave his cloak as collateral, the lender couldn’t keep it overnight.

f.w: thou shalt not sleep with his pledge

chapters.n: Return the cloak by sunset so he has something to sleep in. Showing mercy counts as righteousness before God.

f.w: it shall be righteousness unto thee

f.g: Clothing, here the outer cloak used as a blanket.

chapters.n: Don’t exploit poor hired workers, whether Israelite or foreign.
Pay wages the same day. A poor worker depends on it to eat tonight, and God hears his cry.

f.w: neither shall the sun go down upon it

chapters.n: Each person is responsible for his own crimes. Parents and children cannot be executed for each other’s sins.

f.w: every man shall be put to death for his own sin

chapters.n: Justice for the vulnerable: don’t twist cases against foreigners or orphans, and don’t take a widow’s clothing as collateral.
The motive again: remember that you were slaves and God redeemed you.

f.w: the LORD thy God redeemed thee thence

chapters.n: If a bundle of grain was forgotten in the field, leave it for the poor. This is how Ruth was able to glean in Boaz’s fields.

f.g: A bundle of cut grain stalks.

f.w: for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow

chapters.n: When beating olives from the trees, don’t go back for a second pass — leave the rest for the poor.

f.g: Olives were harvested by striking branches with sticks.

chapters.n: Grape harvest too: don’t strip the vines clean. Leave the remainder for those in need.

f.g: Gather leftover crops after the main harvest.

chapters.n: The chapter closes by repeating the reason: Israel’s memory of slavery should make them compassionate.
When people take a dispute to court, the judges must declare the innocent party in the right and the guilty party in the wrong. Justice means calling things what they are.

f.g: Declare the innocent party not guilty.

chapters.n: Physical punishment, when deserved, was carried out under the judge’s supervision and measured to fit the offense — not left to an angry crowd.
A strict limit of forty lashes protected the offender’s human dignity. Later Jews gave thirty-nine to avoid accidentally exceeding it, which Paul received five times.

f.g: Be degraded or humiliated in your eyes.

chapters.n: An ox treading grain must be allowed to eat as it works. Paul used this verse to teach that those who labor in the gospel deserve support.

f.w: Thou shalt not muzzle the ox

f.g: Walks over harvested grain to separate kernels from husks.

chapters.n: If a man died without children, his brother was to marry the widow. This “levirate” custom protected the widow and kept the family line and land.

f.g: Latin levir — the source of the term “levirate marriage.”

chapters.n: The first son of that marriage would carry on the dead brother’s name and inheritance.

f.w: that his name be not put out of Israel

chapters.n: If the brother refused, the widow could bring the matter publicly to the elders at the city gate.

f.w: to raise up unto his brother a name
f.g: To produce an heir for his brother.

chapters.n: The elders would talk with him; if he still refused, he was free to do so but faced public consequence.
In a public ceremony the widow pulled off his sandal and spat before him, shaming his refusal to care for his brother’s family.

f.w: loose his shoe from off his foot
f.g: A symbol of giving up legal rights to land or family.

chapters.n: His family would be nicknamed “the house of the unsandaled” — a lasting mark of failing to help family.

f.w: The house of him that hath his shoe loosed

chapters.n: A specific case: in a fight, a wife grabs her husband’s attacker by the genitals to stop him.

The punishment was severe because the act threatened his ability to have children — a family’s future. This is the only bodily mutilation penalty in the law; later rabbis interpreted it as a monetary fine.

f.w: thine eye shall not pity her

chapters.n: No cheating with two sets of weights — a heavy one for buying and a light one for selling.

f.g: Two different weights for dishonest trade.
Merchants carried stone weights in a pouch.

chapters.n: The same for measuring containers kept at home: no rigged measures.

f.g: Hebrew “an ephah and an ephah” — two grain measures of different sizes.

chapters.n: Use honest, accurate weights and measures. A just economy brings long life in the land.
God detests dishonest business. Ethics in commerce is part of holiness.
Moses now recalls Amalek’s unprovoked attack on Israel soon after leaving Egypt.
Amalek attacked the stragglers at the rear — the weak, the tired, and the vulnerable — with no fear of God. That cruelty made them a symbol of ruthless evil.

f.g: Attacked those at the back of the line.

chapters.n: Once Israel was at peace, they must wipe out Amalek’s memory. Saul’s failure to carry this out cost him his kingdom.

f.w: blot out the remembrance of Amalek

chapters.n: This ceremony was for the future, once Israel had settled in the promised land. It would mark the fulfillment of God’s promise.

f.w: when thou art come in unto the land

chapters.n: The first produce of the harvest was placed in a basket and carried to the sanctuary, acknowledging that the land and its yield came from God.

f.w: the first of all the fruit of the earth

chapters.n: The worshiper declared to the priest that God had kept his oath — they had arrived in the promised land.
The priest placed the basket before the altar as an offering.

f.g: At the sanctuary’s altar of burnt offering.

chapters.n: A famous creed Israel recited: “A wandering Aramean was my father” — Jacob, who lived in Aram (Syria) and went down to Egypt as a small family that grew into a nation.

f.w: A Syrian ready to perish was my father
f.g: Hebrew “a wandering (or perishing) Aramean” — Jacob, whose family came from Aram.

chapters.n: The Egyptians mistreated and oppressed them with brutal slave labor.
They cried out, and God heard, saw, and understood their misery.
God rescued them with power and miraculous signs.

f.w: with a mighty hand, and with an outstretched arm

chapters.n: And he brought them into this rich land. Each worshiper retold salvation history as their own story — “us,” not just “them.”
Then the worshiper presented the firstfruits, bowed, and worshiped. Gratitude was expressed in a gift.
The ceremony ended in a joyful celebration shared with the Levites and foreigners.

f.w: thou shalt rejoice in every good thing

chapters.n: Every third year the tithe stayed local to feed the needy. After distributing it, the giver made a declaration.
He affirmed before God that he had given the sacred portion to those it belonged to and had obeyed fully.
He swore the tithe hadn’t been defiled — not eaten while ritually unclean in mourning or offered to the dead, as pagans did in their death rituals.

f.w: nor given ought thereof for the dead
f.g: Not used as offerings in funeral cults.

chapters.n: The prayer closes by asking God to look down from heaven and bless his people and their land.

f.w: Look down from thy holy habitation

chapters.n: Moses concludes the law code: obey these laws wholeheartedly, starting today.

f.g: A key phrase in Deuteronomy emphasizing present decision.

chapters.n: Israel had publicly declared the Lord as their God and promised to walk in his ways — a covenant renewal.
In turn, the Lord declared Israel his treasured people. A covenant is a two-way promise.
God promised to raise Israel high in praise, name, and honor — as a holy people that would show the world what he is like.
For the first time in the book, Moses speaks together with Israel’s elders, preparing a ceremony the leaders will carry out after his death.

f.w: Moses with the elders of Israel

chapters.n: After crossing the Jordan, Israel was to set up large stones and coat them with plaster, creating a smooth surface for writing.

f.g: Lime plaster, a known ancient writing surface.

chapters.n: The words of the law would be written on these stones — a public monument declaring Israel lived under God’s covenant in its new land.

f.w: all the words of this law

chapters.n: The location was Mount Ebal, near Shechem in the center of the land.
An altar was to be built of natural stones, untouched by iron tools. Human craftsmanship was not to be added to what God made.

f.w: thou shalt not lift up any iron tool upon them

chapters.n: Whole, uncut stones; on this altar they would offer burnt offerings, fully given to God.
Peace offerings were shared meals — a joyful feast in God’s presence celebrating fellowship with him.

f.g: Fellowship sacrifices shared between God, priest, and worshiper.

chapters.n: The writing must be clear and readable for all.
Moses and the priests declare that this very day Israel has become the Lord’s covenant people.

f.w: this day thou art become the people of the LORD

chapters.n: Being God’s people means obeying his voice and keeping his commandments.

f.w: obey the voice of the LORD

chapters.n: On that same day Moses gave further instructions for the ceremony.
Six tribes descended from Jacob’s wives Leah and Rachel would stand on Mount Gerizim for the blessing.
The other six would stand on Mount Ebal for the curses — mostly the tribes from the handmaids Bilhah and Zilpah, plus Reuben and Zebulun.
The Levites would loudly call out each curse across the valley between the mountains.

f.g: The valley acts as a natural amphitheater.

chapters.n: The first curse: secretly making an idol. Many of these sins are done in private, where only God sees. The people’s “Amen” meant “so be it” — they accepted the covenant’s terms.

f.w: putteth it in a secret place

chapters.n: Treating parents with contempt.
Moving a boundary marker to steal land.
Deliberately misleading a blind person — taking advantage of the helpless.
Denying justice to foreigners, orphans, and widows.
Sexual relations with one’s stepmother.
Bestiality, a perversion associated with pagan practice.
Incest with a sister or half-sister.
Sexual relations with a mother-in-law.
Secret violence — attacking someone where no one sees.
Taking a bribe to kill an innocent person.
A final, all-encompassing curse: failing to uphold the whole law. Paul quoted it to show that no one is justified by the law alone and all need Christ.

f.w: confirmeth not all the words of this law

chapters.n: Moses begins the great chapter of covenant blessings and curses. If Israel listens carefully and obeys, God will raise them above every nation.

f.w: hearken diligently unto the voice of the LORD

chapters.n: Blessings will “overtake” the obedient — chase them down and catch up with them. God’s generosity is pictured as active and eager.

f.w: all these blessings shall come on thee

chapters.n: The blessings cover every place of life — town and countryside alike.

f.g: City and field together form a merism: everywhere.

chapters.n: Children, crops, and livestock would all flourish. Fertility in every sphere was the sign of God’s favor.
The basket for gathering the harvest and the bowl for kneading bread would both be full — daily provision.

f.g: Probably the kneading trough for making bread.

chapters.n: Coming in and going out means all of life’s activities, from morning to night.
Enemies attacking in an organized line would scatter in every direction in panic.

f.g: Scatter in all directions; seven suggests completeness.

chapters.n: God would “command” blessing on barns and work — his word itself brings abundance.
The greatest blessing: Israel would be established as God’s holy people, as he promised by oath.
The nations would recognize that Israel bears the Lord’s name and belongs to him. Latter-day covenant people also take his name upon them.

f.w: called by the name of the LORD

chapters.n: Abundance in goods, children, livestock, and harvests in the land promised to the fathers.
Heaven is pictured as God’s treasury of rain. Faithful Israel would be lenders, not debtors.

f.w: thou shalt lend unto many nations

chapters.n: “The head, and not the tail” — leaders rather than followers, on top rather than underneath.

f.w: the head, and not the tail

chapters.n: The blessings hinge on staying on the straight path and refusing other gods.

f.w: to the right hand, or to the left

chapters.n: Now the curses begin, and they run four times longer than the blessings. Disobedience will bring curses that overtake Israel just as blessings would have.

f.w: all these curses shall come upon thee

chapters.n: The curses mirror the blessings exactly — city and field.

f.w: Cursed shalt thou be in the city

chapters.n: Empty baskets and bread bowls — want instead of plenty.
Children, crops, and herds would all suffer.
Every activity, coming and going, would be under the curse.
Frustration and failure in every effort would follow, because they had forsaken the Lord. The root cause is relational: leaving God.
Plague would cling to them until the land was emptied.
A list of diseases and crop disasters: wasting sickness, fevers, war, scorching wind, and plant mold.

f.g: Crop blight from hot east winds, and grain mildew.

chapters.n: Sky like bronze and ground like iron — hard, rainless, unyielding. Drought would seal both.

f.w: thy heaven that is over thy head shall be brass

chapters.n: Instead of rain, dust storms would blow down from the sky.
The reverse of verse 7: Israel would scatter before its enemies and be taken into all nations.

f.w: removed into all the kingdoms of the earth

chapters.n: The dead would lie unburied, with no one to scare away scavenging birds and animals — a great disgrace in that culture.

f.w: no man shall fray them away

chapters.n: Skin diseases and boils like those sent on Egypt — the oppressor’s plagues turned on Israel.
Mental and spiritual disorientation: confusion, blindness, and panic.
Groping at noon like a blind man in the dark — a picture of hopelessness even in the light. No one would come to rescue.
The exact opposite of the war exemptions in chapter 20: someone else would take your fiancée, your new house, and your vineyard.

f.w: thou shalt build an house, and thou shalt not dwell therein

chapters.n: Livestock seized before your eyes, with no one to help.

f.w: shall not be restored to thee

chapters.n: Children taken into captivity while parents watch helplessly, longing for them every day.

f.w: thine eyes shall look, and fail with longing
f.g: Your eyes will grow weak from watching for them.

chapters.n: A foreign nation would devour all the produce of their labor, leaving them crushed.

f.w: a nation which thou knowest not

chapters.n: The suffering would be so terrible that seeing it would drive them out of their minds.
Painful, incurable sores covering the body from head to foot — like Job’s affliction.

f.w: from the sole of thy foot unto the top of thy head

chapters.n: Even Israel’s future king would go into exile, where they would serve lifeless idols. This came true when Judah’s kings were taken to Babylon.

f.w: thy king which thou shalt set over thee

f.g: Idols made of wood and stone.

chapters.n: Israel would become a shocking example and a joke among the nations.
Sow much, harvest little — locusts would devour the crops.
Vineyards tended with care but ruined by grubs before harvest.
Olive trees would drop their fruit before it ripened — no oil for skin care or cooking.

f.w: thine olive shall cast his fruit

chapters.n: Children would be born only to be carried off into captivity.
Locusts would strip every tree and plant.

f.g: Possibly a specific locust species — the Hebrew word is rare.

chapters.n: Foreigners in the land would rise high while Israel sank low.

f.w: The stranger that is within thee

chapters.n: A total reversal of verses 12–13: Israel would become borrower and tail.

f.w: he shall be the head, and thou shalt be the tail

chapters.n: A summary: these curses will pursue Israel to destruction because they would not listen to God.
These calamities would stand as a lasting sign and warning for Israel’s descendants.

f.w: for a sign and for a wonder

chapters.n: A striking reason: Israel failed to serve God with joy and glad hearts in a time of plenty. Ingratitude is at the root of rebellion.

f.w: with joyfulness, and with gladness of heart

chapters.n: Those who wouldn’t serve God joyfully in abundance would serve enemies in hunger and need, under a crushing iron yoke.

f.w: a yoke of iron upon thy neck

chapters.n: A distant nation would swoop in like an eagle, speaking a foreign language. Fulfilled by Assyria and Babylon, and many see it again in Rome.

f.w: as swift as the eagle flieth
a nation whose tongue thou shalt not understand

chapters.n: A cruel, merciless army that would spare neither elderly nor children.
The invaders would eat up all of Israel’s livestock and crops.
Every walled city Israel trusted in would fall under siege.
Starvation in siege would be so extreme that parents would eat their own children — a horror that actually occurred in Samaria and Jerusalem.

f.w: thou shalt eat the fruit of thine own body

chapters.n: Even the most refined, gentle man would turn hostile toward his own family.

f.g: He will look on them grudgingly or selfishly.

chapters.n: Desperation would destroy natural family love.

f.g: He has nothing else to eat.

chapters.n: The most pampered woman — too delicate to set her foot on the ground — would turn against her husband and children.
She would secretly eat even her own newborn. These verses show how sin’s consequences can destroy the most basic human bonds.
The condition restated: if Israel will not revere God’s glorious and awesome name, Yahweh their God…

f.g: Printed in capitals in KJV for the divine name YHWH, known to Latter-day Saints as Jehovah.

chapters.n: …then their plagues would be extraordinary in severity and duration.
All the diseases of Egypt that Israel once dreaded would come on them.
Even diseases not listed here would come. The list is not exhaustive.

f.w: which is not written in the book of this law

chapters.n: A people once as many as the stars would be reduced to a few — the reversal of the promise to Abraham.

f.w: as the stars of heaven for multitude

chapters.n: Strong language: just as God delighted to bless, he would “delight” in executing judgment — meaning his justice would be as certain as his mercy.

f.w: ye shall be plucked from off the land

chapters.n: Israel would be scattered among all nations and serve idols there. The Book of Mormon affirms this scattering — and the promised gathering.

f.w: the LORD shall scatter thee among all people

chapters.n: No rest, no peace among the nations — only fear, failing eyes, and despair.

f.w: neither shall the sole of thy foot have rest

chapters.n: Life would feel suspended over a pit, with constant fear and no security.

f.w: thy life shall hang in doubt
f.g: Your life will hang by a thread.

chapters.n: So miserable they would wish mornings were evenings and evenings were mornings — anything but the present.
The final curse undoes the Exodus: back to Egypt as slaves, so worthless that no one would even buy them. Josephus reports that Rome sent many Jewish captives to Egypt after A.D. 70.

f.g: Even the slave market would reject you.

chapters.n: A summary heading: these are the terms of a covenant made in Moab, renewing and adding to the one made at Sinai (Horeb) forty years earlier. (In Hebrew Bibles this verse closes chapter 28.)

f.g: The plains east of the Jordan, opposite Jericho.

chapters.n: Moses calls all Israel together and appeals to what they had seen with their own eyes in Egypt.
They had witnessed the plagues and miracles.

f.g: Here “trials” or “tests” — the plagues that tested Pharaoh.

chapters.n: A sobering admission: despite all they’d seen, they still lacked true understanding. Spiritual sight is a gift that must be sought.

f.w: an heart to perceive, and eyes to see, and ears to hear

chapters.n: Moses now voices God’s own words: for forty years their clothes and sandals never wore out.

f.w: your clothes are not waxen old upon you

chapters.n: They lived without ordinary bread and wine, relying on manna, so they would learn to know the Lord as their sustainer.
God gave them victory over the Amorite kings Sihon and Og east of the Jordan.

f.w: Sihon the king of Heshbon, and Og the king of Bashan

chapters.n: That land became the inheritance of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh.
So keep this covenant and prosper. Covenant faithfulness and true success go together.
Everyone stands before God today — leaders and ordinary people alike.

f.w: Ye stand this day all of you
f.g: The whole nation assembled as one.

chapters.n: Even children, wives, and foreigners serving in the camp — down to the woodcutters and water carriers — are included in the covenant.

f.w: from the hewer of thy wood unto the drawer of thy water

chapters.n: The purpose: to enter a covenant sealed by an oath with the Lord.

f.g: Literally “pass into” the covenant — perhaps recalling walking between sacrificial pieces (Genesis 15:17).

chapters.n: Through it Israel becomes God’s people and he becomes their God — the heart of every covenant, promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

f.w: that he may be unto thee a God

chapters.n: This covenant is not only for the people present.
It includes future generations not yet born — and, by extension, all who would later join Israel through covenant.

f.w: him that is not here with us this day

chapters.n: Moses reminds them of their experiences living in Egypt and passing through other nations.

f.w: how we came through the nations

chapters.n: They had seen the idols of those peoples — lifeless objects of wood, stone, silver, and gold.

f.w: their idols, wood and stone, silver and gold

chapters.n: A warning about any person, family, or tribe turning away. Like a poisonous root, one person’s apostasy can spread bitterness through the community.

f.w: a root that beareth gall and wormwood
f.g: Gall and wormwood = bitter, poisonous plants.

chapters.n: The danger of false security: someone hears the curses but tells himself, “I’ll be fine, even if I do what I want.” Self-deception sweeps away the whole.

f.g: An idiom, perhaps “to sweep away the watered with the dry” — ruin everything.

chapters.n: God will not overlook such a person. His jealous anger — protective love for his covenant — will burn against him, and his name will be erased.

f.g: God’s zeal for an exclusive covenant relationship.

chapters.n: That person would be singled out for judgment from among all the tribes.
Future generations and foreigners would see the ruined land and ask what happened.

f.w: the stranger that shall come from a far land

chapters.n: The land would look like Sodom and Gomorrah — burned, salty, barren. Admah and Zeboiim were sister cities destroyed with them.

f.w: the overthrow of Sodom, and Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboim

chapters.n: Nations would ask why God poured out such anger on his own land.

f.w: Wherefore hath the LORD done thus

chapters.n: The answer: they abandoned the covenant God made with them at the Exodus.
They worshiped gods they had no relationship with — gods that had never done anything for them.

f.w: whom he had not given unto them
f.g: Gods not assigned to them — Israel’s portion was the Lord alone (Deuteronomy 32:8-9).

chapters.n: So all the written curses fell upon the land.

f.w: all the curses that are written in this book

chapters.n: God uprooted them and cast them into another land — a prophetic description of exile. The phrase “as it is this day” speaks from the perspective of those who later lived it.

f.w: rooted them out of their land

chapters.n: A beloved verse: some things only God knows, but what he has revealed belongs to us and our children — so we can live it. Latter-day Saints treasure continuing revelation.

f.w: The secret things belong unto the LORD our God

chapters.n: Moses looks far ahead, past the scattering. Even in exile among the nations, Israel will remember these words. Hope is built into the covenant.

f.w: thou shalt call them to mind
f.g: Literally “bring them back to your heart.”

chapters.n: The key is returning — repentance — with heart and soul, for both parents and children.

f.g: Hebrew shuv, “turn back,” the Old Testament word for repentance.

chapters.n: Then God will reverse their fortunes, show compassion, and gather them from every nation. This promise of gathering is central to the Restoration.

f.w: gather thee from all the nations

chapters.n: No one is too far away — even from the ends of the sky, God will bring his people home.

f.g: The farthest horizons — the ends of the earth.

chapters.n: They will possess the land again and be even more prosperous and numerous than their ancestors.
Here God himself changes their hearts. What Israel was told to do (10:16), God promises to do for them — a prophecy of the new covenant and the grace of Christ.
